Revised assessment: The statement highlights robust job gains and low unemployment, but literature suggests the inflation outlook skews risks to the upside and growth risks to the downside. In a New Keynesian Phillips Curve framework, cost-push shocks from supply chains, energy, and the Russia–Ukraine war can make inflation persistent unless expectations remain anchored; the inflation-forecast targeting perspective (Svensson and Woodford, 2005) is consistent with the Committee’s aggressive stance. “Inflation-at-risk” evidence (2024) points to a fat right tail for inflation outcomes in such environments, justifying a faster pace of hikes and balance-sheet reduction. Energy price shocks historically depress activity (VAR-based studies), elevating stagflation risk. Pandemic-driven shifts in consumption baskets (e.g., COVID-19 Inflation Weighting evidence) caution that measured CPI may be biased, but they do not overturn the broad-based nature of price pressures. Emerging work on elevated markups/profits (2023) also implies potential disinflation headwinds. Taken together, the literature tilts this communication more hawkish than neutral: supportive of credibility restoration but with negative implications for near-term growth, outweighing the positive labor data.
